571.quote_or_event: “Be kind to all beings-this is more meritorious than bathing at the sixty-eight sacred shrines of pilgrimage and the giving of charity.”
571.explanation: In his song of the twelve months, Guru Arjan ranks kindness to every living being above all pilgrimages and formal charity.
571.tie_back: The Kural calls kannottam, kindly regard for others, a surpassing beauty by which the world goes on; Guru Arjan likewise places kindness to all beings above every outward religious act.
571.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 136, Raag Maajh (Baarah Maahaa), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
571._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the supreme worth of kindness, though the verse does not claim, as the Kural does, that the world itself is sustained by it.

572.quote_or_event: “Those who forget the Naam, the Name of the Lord, are a burden on the earth.”
572.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose verses the Gurus included in the scripture, says that a life cut off from the divine Name is mere dead weight on the earth.
572.tie_back: The Kural says that people without kindly regard merely exist as a burden on the earth; Farid uses the same image of a worthless life weighing on the earth.
572.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 488, Raag Aasaa, Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
572._accuracy_note: Next-best: the ‘burden on the earth’ image is identical, but Farid's test is remembrance of the Name, not kindly regard for others.

573.quote_or_event: “Among the ragas, Siree Raag is the best, if it inspires you to enshrine love for the True Lord.”
573.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that even the most honoured musical mode is only truly fine when it carries the singer into love; the scripture itself is arranged by raag.
573.tie_back: The Kural asks what use a melody is that does not fit the song, and what use an eye without kindly regard; Guru Amar Das likewise judges music by whether its form carries the right inner feeling.
573.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 83, Siree Raag (Siree Raag ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
573._accuracy_note: Next-best: both judge a musical mode by its fitness to its inner content, but Gurbani's concern is love for God, not kindly regard for others.

574.quote_or_event: “O my eyes, the Lord has infused His Light into you; do not look upon any other than the Lord.”
574.explanation: In Anand Sahib Guru Amar Das tells his eyes that their power of sight is a divine light given for a purpose, and must be used for that purpose.
574.tie_back: The Kural says eyes without kindly regard only seem to be in the face and do no good; Guru Amar Das likewise holds that eyes are worth only what they are used to see.
574.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 922, Raag Raamkalee, Anand Sahib (pauri 36), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
574._accuracy_note: Next-best only: both treat the eyes as having a moral purpose, but for the Guru that purpose is seeing God in all, not showing kindness to people.

575.quote_or_event: “I am adorned with Truth, and I have applied the mascara of the Fear of God to my eyes.”
575.explanation: Speaking as the bride-soul, Guru Arjan says her true adornment is a virtue, and that what she puts on her eyes is reverence for God.
575.tie_back: The Kural calls kindly regard the jewel that adorns the eye, without which eyes are mere sores; Guru Arjan likewise makes a virtue the real ornament of the eyes.
575.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 737, Raag Soohee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
575._accuracy_note: Next-best: the image of a virtue as the eye's ornament matches closely, but the virtue named is reverence for God rather than kindness, and the bride image is spiritual devotion, not romance.

576.quote_or_event: “What can cold do to a stone?”
576.explanation: Guru Nanak uses the stone that feels no cold as an image of the person on whom nothing outside can make an impression.
576.tie_back: The Kural says those who have eyes yet never look kindly on others are like trees rooted in the soil, with form but no feeling; Guru Nanak's unfeeling stone makes the same point about outward form with no inner response.
576.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 143, Raag Maajh (Maajh ki Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
576._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the image of insensibility is parallel, but Guru Nanak's verse is about people unmoved by spiritual teaching, not about lack of kindness to others.

577.quote_or_event: “Do not call them blind, who have no eyes in their face. They alone are blind, O Nanak, who wander away from their Lord and Master.”
577.explanation: Guru Angad redefines blindness: the truly blind are not those without physical sight but those who have strayed from God.
577.tie_back: The Kural says those without kindly regard are really eyeless, and those who truly have eyes always have it; Guru Angad makes the same move of redefining sight and blindness in moral terms.
577.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 954, Raag Raamkalee (Raamkalee ki Vaar, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
577._accuracy_note: Strong structural fit: both redefine true sight morally, though Guru Angad's criterion is closeness to God rather than kindly regard for others.

578.quote_or_event: “They are kind to all beings; they have overpowered the five thieves.”
578.explanation: Guru Arjan describes the holy as joining kindness to all beings with firm mastery over lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride.
578.tie_back: The Kural says the world belongs to those who show kindly regard without letting their duty be spoiled; Guru Arjan likewise pairs kindness with a discipline that it is never allowed to weaken.
578.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1357, Salok Sehskritee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
578._accuracy_note: Next-best only: kindness held together with self-mastery is a fair parallel, but the verse does not address the Kural's specific limit, that favour must not corrupt a ruler's justice.

579.quote_or_event: “Where there is greed, there is death. Where there is forgiveness, there is God Himself.”
579.explanation: Bhagat Kabir places forgiveness at the highest level, as the very place where God is present.
579.tie_back: The Kural calls it the highest virtue to bear patiently with those whose nature is to hurt us; Kabir likewise exalts forgiveness above all, as the dwelling of God Himself.
579.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1372, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
579._accuracy_note: Reasonable to strong fit on forgiveness as the highest quality, though Kabir does not specify forbearance toward those who actively injure us.

580.quote_or_event: “Your Will seems so sweet to me; whatever You do, is pleasing to me.”
580.explanation: Guru Arjan prays to accept whatever God sends, bitter or sweet, as pleasing; Sikh tradition remembers him for keeping this acceptance through his torture and martyrdom in 1606.
580.tie_back: The Kural praises those who, for the sake of courtesy, will calmly drink poison poured for them by a friend; Guru Arjan's acceptance of whatever comes as sweet is the Sikh counterpart of such calm endurance.
580.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 713, Raag Todee, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
580._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Guru Arjan accepts the divine Will, not harm from a friend for courtesy's sake, and Sikh teaching does not commend submitting to a friend's wrongdoing.
